1. Low-JA/JP spot-check rule — operationalised and executed

Added to eng.md § Monitoring Loop: whenever (JA/JP%) reads below 30%, dispatch an SA to briefly review the most recent non-applying ARs. Executed immediately (rate was 17%, JP=88/JA=15 at the time): the SA reviewed the 8 most recent skips against the candidate profile and playbook.md.

This confirms exactly the caveat you raised: the low rate this runtime is job-mismatch, not an AJAP bug.

2. Compaction hedge — research findings + proposal (NOT implemented)

What exists today: nothing cockpit-specific

Dispatched an SA to check AJAP_dir/CLAUDE.md, eng.md, AJAP_inv/CLAUDE.md, and the root dupbus-ceztuc-7cufVe/CLAUDE.md § 5 compaction protocol. Findings:

  • The ONLY compaction-aware exception anywhere is #sprint's slog_[TS].md mechanism (root CLAUDE.md § 5.8) — an append-only per-task log that, if found among the 5 most-recent files in the session folder, lets a sprint resume from its last block instead of halting. It's scoped to #sprint task work and keyed to the dupbus sessions/ folder — a structure #seek/#eng doesn't use (comms live in AJAP_inv/[YYYY]/[YYYYMM]/).
  • Absent that exception, the BASELINE behavior (root CLAUDE.md § 5) is: emit 🚨 Compaction Detected —— stopped all tasks., halt everything, and wait for the user's instruction.
  • This baseline directly conflicts with the cockpit's own "never summon the user, run fully autonomously" rule (AJAP_dir/CLAUDE.md § Rules, inherited by eng.md). Nothing today resolves that conflict — it's an open gap, not a decided policy.

What would actually be at risk

None of the following is currently persisted anywhere (CONTROL.md, progress.log, status.jsonl, usage.jsonl, eng_report_*.md — checked):

  • **Which eng_report_*.md files were written this session** — needed by the sesL-Wake Reconciliation and ALWAYS-REPORT rules, both of which scan "since session start." Your own example was exactly right: post-compaction, I'd have no way to tell which reports are mine-this-session vs. inherited from earlier, and would fall back to the "last 24h" guess — noisy on a busy day, and could either re-report something already covered or miss something genuinely new.
  • The runtime-start timestamp used for since= in every ledger query this session (session_applied_count/session_submitted_count) — without it, the 🎯/🚀 baseline breaks (would either reset to 0 or silently pick up a stale/wrong prior runtime).
  • Which questions.md entries were already raised this runtime — could re-raise the same batch, which the protocol explicitly says wastes tokens and shouldn't happen mid-run.
  • Which persistent Monitors are armed and what they watch — the SELF-CHECK step already handles a Monitor dying normally, but post-compaction I might not even remember I'm SUPPOSED to have 5 of them armed, let alone which task IDs they are.
  • The last-reported cumulative 🎯/🚀 numbers — needed to avoid double-counting or gapping the next report.

Proposed hedge (your call on whether to implement)

Minimisation (reduce how often this bites, not eliminate it):

  • Keep routine per-notification chat replies terse (already the practice) — the bulk of context growth here is the AR-watch/heartbeat/progress-line acknowledgment stream, which is also the user-visible audit trail, so I wouldn't compress that away; but I could periodically consolidate a long run of routine "same event, already covered" replies into a single digest line instead of one reply per Monitor duplicate, which is pure repetition today.
  • Actively externalise the at-risk state (below) to a file at natural checkpoints rather than only holding it in conversation memory — this is really the same fix as the sentinel, just framed as "write it before you need it" rather than "recover it after."

Post-compaction sentinel + protocol (mirrors #sprint's slog pattern, adapted for the cockpit):

  • A new append-only file, e.g. AJAP_code/runtime/cockpit_slog_[runtime_start_TS].md (runtime-scoped state, so it lives alongside the other runtime/ files rather than as an AJAP_inv/ comms artifact) — one block per meaningful checkpoint: runtime-start TS; each Monitor armed (task ID + what it watches) whenever armed/re-armed; each eng_report_*.md written (filename + one-line gist) whenever written; playbook question numbers raised, whenever raised; the latest 🎯/🚀 baseline, on each report.
  • A cockpit-specific compaction exception in eng.md (and really AJAP_dir/CLAUDE.md, since most of the at-risk state — questions raised, 🎯/🚀 baseline, Monitor IDs — is coordinator-level, not #eng-only): on the 🚨 PostCompact sentinel, instead of halting and waiting for the user (which the cockpit's own autonomy rule already forbids), read the slog's latest block, recover the 5 items above, re-arm any dead Monitors, and resume — emitting a brief 🚨 Compaction recovered — resumed from cockpit_slog line so you can see it happened, but never blocking on you.
  • This explicitly needs your sign-off before I build it, since it means the cockpit would OVERRIDE the generic § 5 halt-and-wait baseline for itself — a real policy call, not just a doc tidy-up. Flagging that tension rather than deciding it unilaterally.

3 & 4. Corrections applied

  • Moved the display-flip "Known Quirks" note from eng.md to AJAP_inv/CLAUDE.md — you were right, #eng reads the latter but #inv never reads the former.
  • Broadened the sesL-Wake Reconciliation rule: it now scans for ANY file change (not just defect-fixes), except routine CONTROL.md anchor-steering. Also added the new ALWAYS-REPORT rule: any user-message-led file change gets its own eng_report_*.md live, in the same turn — this message's own changes are the first thing filed under it (eng_report_202607160645.md).

## Curiosity on Naming (Verified, Not Guessed)

218. The mechanism is called **prompt caching** —— a real, specific Anthropic API feature, and I checked current docs rather than relying on memory
- 218.1. What it is: a shared IDENTICAL prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, baked-in documents) gets cached server-side; a later call reusing that SAME prefix within the cache's TTL gets it back at roughly 10% of normal input-token cost and much faster time-to-first-token. It is NOT "read once, then clone 5 ways" —— every call is still its own independent request; caching just makes the SHARED portion cheap on repeat, not free-and-singular.
- 218.2. TTL note (dated, worth knowing): Anthropic quietly dropped the default TTL from 60min to 5min in early 2026 —— matches this session's own tooling documentation elsewhere.
- 218.3. NOT exclusive to the Agent SDK —— it's a Messages-API-level feature (`cache_control` breakpoints), so the raw API, the Agent SDK, and Claude Code can all use it in principle.
- 218.4. A genuine correction to what you were told before: Claude Code's own Agent-tool-dispatched subagents (exactly what I use to dispatch every SA this session) have prompt caching HARDCODED OFF by default —— a known, currently-open issue (anthropics/claude-code#29966). So dispatching 5 ordinary SAs to each read file X gets ZERO caching benefit today —— each one is fully fresh, no shared-read efficiency at all. The mechanism that DOES share cache is FORKING a session (a fork inherits the parent's cached prompt; its first request is a genuine cache hit) —— so your "similar to forking a CC session" instinct was more literally correct than the "just caching" framing suggests: forking is the specific, named path that gets the benefit; plain multi-SA dispatch (what I actually do) currently does not.
- 218.5. Whether AJAP's own SA1/SA3 raw `claude_agent_sdk.query()` calls get ANY caching benefit is genuinely uncertain from documentation alone —— a March-2026 SDK feature request notes the current `ClaudeAgentOptions`/Bedrock path doesn't support injecting `cache_control` metadata. I did not verify this against the exact SDK version installed in this repo; flagging as an open question rather than guessing, if you want certainty later.
- 218.6. Sources: [Prompt caching — Claude Platform Docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching), [Create custom subagents — Claude Code Docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents), [Agent SDK subagents have prompt caching disabled by default — GitHub #29966](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/29966), [Prompt Caching Support in Claude Agent SDK — GitHub #626](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python/issues/626)

Curiosity on Naming (Verified, Not Guessed)

  • The mechanism is called prompt caching —— a real, specific Anthropic API feature, and I checked current docs rather than relying on memory
  • 218.1. What it is: a shared IDENTICAL prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, baked-in documents) gets cached server-side; a later call reusing that SAME prefix within the cache's TTL gets it back at roughly 10% of normal input-token cost and much faster time-to-first-token. It is NOT "read once, then clone 5 ways" —— every call is still its own independent request; caching just makes the SHARED portion cheap on repeat, not free-and-singular.
  • 218.2. TTL note (dated, worth knowing): Anthropic quietly dropped the default TTL from 60min to 5min in early 2026 —— matches this session's own tooling documentation elsewhere.
  • 218.3. NOT exclusive to the Agent SDK —— it's a Messages-API-level feature (cache_control breakpoints), so the raw API, the Agent SDK, and Claude Code can all use it in principle.
  • 218.4. A genuine correction to what you were told before: Claude Code's own Agent-tool-dispatched subagents (exactly what I use to dispatch every SA this session) have prompt caching HARDCODED OFF by default —— a known, currently-open issue (anthropics/claude-code#29966). So dispatching 5 ordinary SAs to each read file X gets ZERO caching benefit today —— each one is fully fresh, no shared-read efficiency at all. The mechanism that DOES share cache is FORKING a session (a fork inherits the parent's cached prompt; its first request is a genuine cache hit) —— so your "similar to forking a CC session" instinct was more literally correct than the "just caching" framing suggests: forking is the specific, named path that gets the benefit; plain multi-SA dispatch (what I actually do) currently does not.
  • 218.5. Whether AJAP's own SA1/SA3 raw claude_agent_sdk.query() calls get ANY caching benefit is genuinely uncertain from documentation alone —— a March-2026 SDK feature request notes the current ClaudeAgentOptions/Bedrock path doesn't support injecting cache_control metadata. I did not verify this against the exact SDK version installed in this repo; flagging as an open question rather than guessing, if you want certainty later.
  • 218.6. Sources: Prompt caching — Claude Platform Docs, Create custom subagents — Claude Code Docs, Agent SDK subagents have prompt caching disabled by default — GitHub #29966, Prompt Caching Support in Claude Agent SDK — GitHub #626

## Curious Question (The Two Moons)

177. Solved —— same code, different font-fallback chains
- 177.1. The icon is the plain text glyph ☾ (U+263E) set via textContent, and the button inherits the page's font stack —— NONE of those fonts actually contain that codepoint.
- 177.2. So each viewer falls through to its OWN engine-internal fallback list: Safari (full macOS WebKit) lands on the system symbol font's bold solid crescent; the Claude app's embedded webview is a different rendering context w/ a different fallback chain and lands on a thin outline-style face.
- 177.3. Both stay monochrome because U+263E defaults to text-presentation (correctly no colour-emoji 🌙 in either) —— but text-presentation leaves the exact SHAPE to whichever fallback font wins, which is precisely what diverges.

## Design Pcmd & Anthropic Skills (Discussion, Per Your Ask)

137. My take: hybrid —— pcmd stays canonical, skills become the trigger
- 137.1. A standalone design pcmd is warranted: §9.05 colours + layout/typography preferences + HTML self-containment + the WCAG bar + numbered/Title-Case interplay currently live scattered (c.md, this QA's lessons) —— one `universal/design.md` would collect them.
- 137.2. But your review.real pain is TRIGGERING, not content: §7 conditional rows rely on the model actively remembering to check them —— coding.md sat unread for weeks; a design.md would suffer identically.
- 137.3. Anthropic skills fix exactly that: a skill's description is matched by the harness and surfaced automatically (and `/name` makes it user-invocable) —— the trigger becomes infrastructure instead of model discipline; token cost is near-zero until invoked.
- 137.4. Recommended shape: thin SKILL SHIMS whose whole body is "read `universal/[name].md` and follow it" —— content stays in your pcmd ecosystem (one source of truth, GH-versioned, OTG-readable), the skill only guarantees the read fires; start w/ `coding` + `design`, measure trigger reliability over a few sessions, then decide whether to migrate more (or fully).
- 137.5. Caveats: skills live per-project/user under `.claude/` (a second place to maintain —— the shim pattern keeps that surface tiny); descriptions need careful wording (they ARE the trigger); worth one calibration session.
- 137.6. Per your wording ("a discussion should be set out"), nothing built —— green-light and I'll create `universal/design.md` + the two shims next turn.

New-View Problem —— Window 1 Built (Re Your Spec)

  • What was built
  • 128.1. browser/navigator.py: ONE dedicated thread owns the shared results window (own logged-in profile clone; seats talk via a queue —— Playwright objects never cross threads).
  • 128.2. The correctness core: each results page is enumerated ONCE and both seats consume that IDENTICAL snapshot (cards + canonical job URLs + applied/saved states) —— volatility can no longer split the seats' views; they truly meet in the middle (ledger claims still arbitrate the last card).

  • 128.4. Layout: your arithmetic holds —— Window 1 + one workspace window per seat (Tab 2 job post, Tab 3 interactions, Tab 4⁺ research), all 960×1080 stacked on Display 4's right half; 3 windows = 2 seats, 4 = any 3rd seat (grace replacement, ⏳ pickup seat, or drain).

55. What AR footnotes actually are (self-contained, no need to read the long file): application records ("AR" —— the `.md` file AJAP writes per job application) now cite their sources. Any factual claim in an AR that came from an EXTERNAL source (the employer's official site, LinkedIn, Glassdoor, etc.) gets a small marker like `[^01]` right after the sentence, and each section that used any markers ends with a matching list `[^01]: <source URL>`. The numbering is meant to be 2 digits and to keep counting up across the WHOLE document (so if §1 uses `[^01]`–`[^05]`, §2's first marker is `[^06]`, not `[^01]` again). §6 (the cover letter, which is the candidate's own words) never gets a marker. The stated purpose was auditability —— e.g. before an interview, you can trace exactly which claim came from which URL.
56. How it is built: entirely as an instruction TEXT inside the prompt that asks the AI worker to write the AR (`agents/prompts.py`) —— there is no code anywhere that actually CHECKS the AI followed the numbering rule correctly (no verification that markers are sequential, that every marker has a matching URL line, that none appear in §6, etc.).
57. THE ISSUE a dispatched SA found (this turn, auditing pt 12): I had judged that gap "acceptable" —— same as how the rest of the AR's bullet-point formatting is also unenforced prompt-only text. The SA disagreed and I now agree with it: that analogy doesn't hold, because a malformed BULLET is merely untidy, but a malformed FOOTNOTE (numbers reset mid-document, a marker with no matching URL, etc.) silently breaks the exact traceability the feature exists for —— and this codebase already puts a deterministic check on a comparable auditability property elsewhere (the linter verifies CL figures trace back to real profile facts). The SA's suggestion: add a small check (roughly 15 lines of regex logic) to the linter that verifies the footnote numbering is well-formed before an AR is accepted. This is currently UNFIXED —— flagging it to you as an open item, your call whether to action it now or later.

## Re 392 (Claim-Awareness + Line-3 Furthest-Qi + a Hard Self-Audit)

410. Re 392.1, confirmed with code: the per-card ledger `claim()` IS the cross-seat awareness. When seat 1 reaches a card seat 0 already holds, `claim()` returns False (a single atomic INSERT-OR-IGNORE; only the first claimant wins) and seat 1 skips it and moves on. So your "WRONG" case cannot happen —— two seatsmodel-switch neverdiagnostics. work the same card.
411. Re 392.3, the furthest-Qi Line-3 mirror is built: whoever advances to a further Qi writes Line 3 (no waiting for the straggler); a user edit jumps every seat.
412. 🔴 HONESTY FOR YOUR AUDIT: after building it I ran a 3-perspective adversarial self-review of the whole pool (Line-3, two-ends, grace). It found REAL bugs in my own code. I fixed the confirmed high-severity ones rather than ship them:
- 412.1. Line-3 had FOUR override races: a furthest write could clobber an unread user edit (jump lost to zero seats); a grace-replacement seat could resurrect a long-consumed jump; a seat already on the jumped-to Qi would spuriously re-jump after advancing; a repeat edit to the same Qi was ignored. REBUILT the mechanism (a monotonic jump-sequence + a guard that never lets a mirror write erase an unread edit + mirror-state updated only on a successful write + missing-file creation) —— all four are now closed and pinned by 4 regression tests encoding the exact failing scenarios.
- 412.2. A card abandoned by a STOP or a jump was being ledger-claimed first and then leaked (blocked ~12h). FIXED: the claim now happens AFTER the STOP/jump gates.
- 412.3. I corrected a false comment: two seats can drift MORE than 1 card apart only in the pathological case where one card runs the full 29-min grace —— then Line 3 (furthest-wins) over-reports. That is inherent to your no-barrier §392.3 choice; flagging itGrouped so you can decidepoint ifme youat wantwhichever ato light cap on how far ahead a seat may run.re-audit.*

Thoughts on All; GH-History Forensics; Sprint Follows

Re 320 (Why GH Lost the Swap History)

  • Root cause: git stores NO rename records at all —— only snapshots; every history view (GH's, git log --follow, git_history.py) RE-DETECTS renames at display time by content similarity, and each tool draws its own line.
  • 345.1. queue.md's hop was a PURE rename (R100, zero content change) —— GH bridged it, hence its 3 commits.
  • 345.2. CONTROL.md's hop was rename + rewrite IN THE SAME COMMIT (I re-wrote the explainer whilst moving it): the 5-line file changed so much that even a 5% similarity threshold fails to pair the delete w/ the add —— git itself recorded D + A, so GH sees a brand-new file (1 commit). My fault, and a lesson now codified (345.4).
  • 345.3. git_history.py beat GH on both because its deepening + basename fallbacks bridge what similarity alone cannot; nothing is lost in git's objects —— only the VIEWS differ.
  • 345.4. Doctrine adopted for ALL future moves (incl. the migration): NEVER combine a move w/ content edits in one commit —— edit, commit, then git mv, commit (a pure move = R100 = bridgeable by every tool forever); added to migration.md this sprint.

Re 323 (appearance_state.json "Zombie" Change)

  • Nothing zombie-ran; full chain reconstructed w/ evidence, in order:
  • 346.1. The file has been TRACKED since commit 8c43369 (your 0528 commit): the then runtime-local .gitignore had NO *.json rule (the dark engine —— and this file —— were born only hours earlier), so it slipped into git.
  • 346.2. Your 316.4 git rm -r --cached DID stage its removal (your paste shows it), but your commit 631b736 carried every runtime deletion EXCEPT this one —— GH Desktop re-staged from the working tree, and this one file's working copy was NOT ignored at that moment, so the staged deletion was silently dropped and it stayed tracked.
  • 346.3. Your CIIW is right that the root .gitignore rule covers it (AJAP_code/runtime/*.json, verified w/ git check-ignore --no-index) —— but ignore rules NEVER affect already-tracked files, which is exactly why changes still surface.
  • 346.4. The DARK → LIGHT write itself: MY doing, not a zombie —— the post-compaction recovery you ordered ran the test suite at 202607082109, and one code path (appearance mirroring per card) writes the REAL state file even under pytest; it recorded your fresh light-mode switch. A test-hygiene bug: fixed this sprint (tests now write a sandboxed state file).
  • 346.5. What you saw 2057~2203 was therefore the UNCOMMITTED working-tree diff in GitHub Desktop (your commit 84fc86d at 205758 only carried an older clock: true→false flip —— still DARK); GH web never showed LIGHT.
  • 346.6. CONTROL.md staying DARK is CORRECT behaviour: Line 2 is mirrored per card by the RUNNING programme only; the state json is merely the engine's memory file. No background code exists —— when the programme is dead, nothing of AJAP runs.
  • 346.7. Verdict: the mirroring design is expected + kept; the GH visibility was the bug. Fixes: (a) test sandboxing (346.4); (b) I staged the one-off git rm --cached AJAP_code/runtime/appearance_state.json for you —— your next commit finalises it, GH then shows the file as removed from tracking (it STAYS on disk, exactly like the 316.4 batch) and never surfaces again.

Re 325 (Lesson + --psl-done Enforcement)

  • Lesson held post-compaction (re-derive consumers from the new single source of truth; pre-empt rather than patch) —— and applying it to your 325.1 immediately surfaced TWO extra gaps beyond the doc one you spotted:
  • 347.1. Your finding confirmed: psl.md (the file a #psl session actually reads today) never mentions --psl-done; only psl_new.md does. Fix: a concise mandate block added to psl.md (promotion MUST run --psl-done; NEVER hand-move a PSL_ pending AR) + the same prohibition line added to psl_new.md; no long prose.
  • 347.2. Pre-empted gap A (defence in depth): even w/ docs, a forgetful session could still hand-move a file —— so the mirror now HEALS it: at every programme start, a ledger row stuck on Pending whose AR file now sits under applied/ is updated to PslApplied (invisible to ajap_logs by construction) + listed in the mirror report. Sabotage class closed even when the rule is ignored.
  • 347.3. Pre-empted gap B (real bug found): --psl-done wrote its ledger row w/ an ad-hoc key format instead of the canonical compact key —— the mirror would then MISS it and add a duplicate MirrorApplied row at next start (harmless to analytics but dirty). Fixed to use the canonical key.

Re 326.1 (Ledger vs Files)

  • Confirmed: ajap_logs.py reads ONLY the ledger (read-only SQLite; outcomes Applied/Skipped/Pending counted, all else excluded); no gcl file scan remains in its collection path.
  • 348.1. Silent-skip dedupe in a RUN is BOTH + a page backstop: (a) ledger lookup (raw job key AND canonical compact key, 30-day window); (b) an init-time filename scan of the live applied/pending/skipped folders of BOTH seek/gcl and AJAP_repo/gcl; (c) the "you applied on" page-text gate as final backstop regardless of key mismatches.
  • 348.2. The 3k⁺ old ARs do NOT need ledger import: the dedupe window is 30 days by design (K6), so ancient ARs cannot block anything anyway; the 391 already-baked LegacyImport keys + the seek/gcl filename scan cover the live window until migration; and the page gate catches any stragglers. Your 1.5MB estimate is right but the import would buy nothing.

Re 328.1 + 328.2 (Backup Contingency; Ledger Size)

The ~0.5KB/row estimate stands (includes indices/overhead), so 328.2's 25MB/heavy-year projection is unchanged.

Re 336 + 339.10 (git_history.py vs GH —— the Forensic Surprise)

  • I generalised the script as ordered, but the investigation (all 15 SHAs checked locally) overturned the premise —— GH's "extra 15" for ProjectSummary are provably NOT this file's history:
  • 353.1. All 15 SHAs exist locally and are on main —— nothing is missing from the clone (and d851cfc from query 313 was a transposition typo of d851fcf, which is why my rev-parse test wrongly concluded "not local"; my apology —— I should have tried near-variants).
  • 353.2. MGTK751_ProjectSummary_00.md was born as a FRESH 42-line file in f75d8f8 (its blob exists nowhere earlier); zoom_w1 was NEVER renamed into it —— in that same commit MGTK751_zoom_w1.md was purely renamed zoom/ → Seminars/ and it STILL EXISTS there today.
  • 353.3. GH's pre-f75d8f8 chain is two content-free "structural guesses" deep: hop 1 to zoom/MGTK751_zoom_w1.md (shares 1 byte of content, ~0.001%), hop 2 from d851fcf to backup/Claude/preferences.md —— an unrelated Claude prompt doc whose 14 commits (23a8fde "Create preferences.md", 20260323, onwards) are the "full history since 20260323" you saw. GH's view here is semantically bogus, not more robust.
  • 353.4. Verified exhaustively: rename AND copy detection down to a 1% threshold still terminates at f75d8f8 —— no content-based method can ever bridge it, because there is genuinely nothing to bridge.
  • 353.5. Your generalisation demand is still implemented —— a "structural bridge" fallback that reproduces GH's behaviour (when a chain dead-ends at a plain ADD, hop to the best filename-matching path that vanished in that same commit, repeatedly): git_history.py now pulls AT LEAST what GH shows, but unlike GH it MARKS each such hop as a labelled low-confidence bridge, so you always know where verified content lineage ends and GH-style guessing begins.
  • 353.6. Re 339.10's real fear (the cp/ migration): reassurance w/ precision —— rename detection is CONTENT-based, not name-based, so even a COMPLETE basename change survives perfectly IF the move commit is pure (100% similarity always pairs); partial renames and folder moves likewise. The only killers are (a) rename + heavy edit in ONE commit and (b) delete-then-recreate across commits. Follow 345.4's move-only-commit doctrine and every dissertation/ history survives on both GH and the script; and moving CPs within the SAME repo (root → cp/) has no cross-repo loss at all.

Re 339.1 + 339.9 (Qi Line; Headless Probe)

  • Re 339.1, "fight over it" meant: parallel seats partition the Qis between them, and two seats both mirroring Line 3 would overwrite each other's value every few seconds —— solved from day one by seat 0 alone owning the line.
  • 354.1. HOWEVER, your question made me re-audit the JUMP side and it exposed a real gap I had not disclosed: only seat 0 READ the line too, so in pool mode your manual Qi edit was honoured only if the target sat in seat 0's partition —— an edit targeting another seat's Qis was silently swallowed and even overwritten by seat 0's mirror.
  • 354.2. Fixed this sprint: every seat now reads Line 3 and jumps when the target is in ITS partition (whoever owns it reacts; seat 0 still solely writes the mirror, and only re-asserts over a Qi that exists in NOBODY's queue). Single-seat/#psl behaviour is unchanged.

## Re 271 (ledger mechanics + the mirror script)

300. Re 271.2, confirmed —— the ledger is NEVER fully read:
- 300.1. SQLite = a single-file database; queries use an INDEX (like a book's index) to jump straight to the matching row —— reading 1 row costs the same whether the table holds 500 or 500,000.
- 300.2. Why SQLite here: zero-install (built into Python), one file, safe concurrent writers (our two seats), atomic writes that survive crashes; cons: not human-readable (needs a query tool) and binary (git-unfriendly —— why it is git-ignored).

300. Re 271.2, confirmed —— the ledger is NEVER fully read:
- 300.1. SQLite = a single-file database; queries use an INDEX (like a book's index) to jump straight to the matching row —— reading 1 row costs the same whether the table holds 500 or 500,000.
- 300.2. Why SQLite here: zero-install (built into Python), one file, safe concurrent writers (our two seats), atomic writes that survive crashes; cons: not human-readable (needs a query tool) and binary (git-unfriendly —— why it is git-ignored).

27.not 4.2the (how can PD/orchestrator be NOT an LLMpackage) and stillhistorical hitrecords (slog/sprint report say `ajap/`; they describe the goal): the orchestrator owns CONTROL FLOW, not JUDGEMENT.
- 27.1. Deterministic code (the PD) does only what code is reliable at: read the queue, spawn a worker, start timers, hold approvals, write records, retry, recover on restart. None of that needs intelligence —— and BECAUSE it's code, it cannot forget, drift, or compact. That is the whole point: the failure classes lived in the LLM doing orchestration; move orchestration to code and they vanish.
- 27.2. ALL judgement stays with LLM calls, NOT dumped on one auditor:
  - 27.2.1. Worker (SA1, LLM): research, the M1`~`M7 scoring REASONING, CL writing, page/portal Q&A —— every "is this a fit / what do I write / what does this field want" call.
  - 27.2.2. Auditor (SA3, LLM): the semantic CL review you correctly say code can't do —— false claims, stance/emphasis, overall quality, decision precision.
  - 27.2.3. Code (linter v2): only the deterministic slice —— dashes/`+`, section numbers, P.S. tail, employer-name match, figure-vs-profile facts, salary/notice answers.
- 27.3. So it's code orchestrates → LLMs judge → code verifies-what's-verifiable. The PD being code doesn't remove intelligence; it removes the intelligence from the one place (the loop) where drift was fatal.

28. 4.4 (fork SA1 once-primed, then per-card forks with full context, no re-reading): you are RIGHT, and it converges with what I proposed.
- 28.1. Your insight —— SA1 needs no session continuity; card 2 need not know card 1 —— is exactly the property that makes fresh-per-card safe. Confirmed.
- 28.2. Two implementations of the SAME principle:
  - 28.2.1. Your fork model: prime a session on the context once, fork per card. The SDK supports session resume/fork; prompt-caching makes the shared prefix ~free on each fork.
  - 28.2.2. My scoped-prompt model: the orchestrator hands each worker only its slice (CL rules + profile + rubric verdict + THIS job's text), never the 111KB.
- 28.3. Difference: mine gives the worker LESS (only what one card needs) so it's even leaner; yours gives the worker the FULL primed context cheaply. Both avoid re-reading; both give fresh context per card. We'll use whichever measures cheaper at P6.1 —— likely a hybrid (fork a small primed base that holds the stable CL/profile rules, inject the per-card job text).
- 28.4. Correction to my earlier framing (r2 pt 21): "fresh worker doesn't re-read" is right, but your "read once then fork" is the cleaner mental model —— adopted.

29. 4.6 (let a struggling SA1 keep going whilst PD moves on): yes, and this is the design's strength.
- 29.1. Because each worker owns ONE card, a worker stuck on a hard portal is isolated —— it cannot stall the system. The PD watches its token use and either lets it finish or kills it on a ceiling, meanwhile advancing the queue.
- 29.2. Serial mode (default, 1 worker): trivially fine —— PD just times out and re-queues.
- 29.3. Your worry (multiple struggling SA1s under parallel scaling): handled by the worker-POOL abstraction (scaffolded, not active). Each worker is independent; a struggler is one occupied slot; the PD applies the same retire triggers per worker. No SA2/SA3 fan-out problem because SA2/SA3 are code, scaling to N workers for free.past).

- 27.1. Deterministic code (the PD) does only what code is reliable at: read the queue, spawn a worker, start timers, hold approvals, write records, retry, recover on restart. None of that needs intelligence —— and BECAUSE it's code, it cannot compact;forget, workersdrift, getor compact. That is the whole point: the failure classes lived in the LLM doing orchestration; move orchestration to code and they vanish.
- 27.2. ALL judgement stays with LLM calls, NOT dumped on one auditor:
  - 27.2.1. Worker (SA1, LLM): research, the M1`~`M7 scoring REASONING, CL writing, page/portal Q&A —— every "is this a fit / what do I write / what does this field want" call.

- 27.3. So it's code orchestrates → LLMs judge → code verifies-what's-verifiable. The PD being code doesn't remove intelligence; it removes the intelligence from the one place (the loop) where drift was fatal.

28. 4.4 (fork SA1 once-primed, then per-card forks with full context, no re-reading): you are RIGHT, and it converges with what I proposed.
- 28.1. Your insight —— SA1 needs no session continuity; card 2 need not know card 1 —— is exactly the property that makes fresh-per-card safe. Confirmed.
- 28.2. Two implementations of the SAME principle:
  - 28.2.1. Your fork model: prime a session on the context once, fork per card. The SDK supports session resume/fork; prompt-caching makes the shared prefix ~free on each fork.
  - 28.2.2. My scoped-prompt model: the orchestrator hands each worker only its slice (CL rules + profile + rubric verdict + THIS job's text), never the 111KB.
- 28.3. Difference: mine gives the worker LESS (only what one card needs) so it's even leaner; yours gives the worker the FULL primed context cheaply. Both avoid re-reading; both give fresh bounded context per card;card. stateWe'll use whichever measures cheaper at P6.1 —— likely a hybrid (fork a small primed base that holds the stable CL/profile rules, inject the per-card job text).
- 28.4. Correction to my earlier framing (r2 pt 21): "fresh worker doesn't re-read" is persistedright, but your "read once then fork" is the cleaner mental model —— adopted.

29. 4.6 (let a struggling SA1 keep going whilst PD moves on): yes, and this is the design's strength.
- 29.1. Because each worker owns ONE card, a worker stuck on a hard portal is isolated —— it cannot stall the system. The PD watches its token use and either lets it finish or kills it on a ceiling, meanwhile advancing the queue.
- 29.2. Serial mode (default, 1 worker): trivially fine —— PD just times out and re-queues.
- 29.3. Your worry (multiple struggling SA1s under parallel scaling): handled by the worker-POOL abstraction (scaffolded, not active). Each worker is independent; a struggler is one occupied slot; the PD applies the same retire triggers per worker. No SA2/SA3 fan-out problem because SA2/SA3 are code, scaling to disk.N workers for free.

Re 4 —— Architecture

  • 4.2 (how can PD/orchestrator be NOT an LLM and still hit the goal): the orchestrator owns CONTROL FLOW, not JUDGEMENT.
  • 27.1. Deterministic code (the PD) does only what code is reliable at: read the queue, spawn a worker, start timers, hold approvals, write records, retry, recover on restart. None of that needs intelligence —— and BECAUSE it's code, it cannot forget, drift, or compact. That is the whole point: the failure classes lived in the LLM doing orchestration; move orchestration to code and they vanish.
  • 27.2. ALL judgement stays with LLM calls, NOT dumped on one auditor:
  • 27.2.1. Worker (SA1, LLM): research, the M1~M7 scoring REASONING, CL writing, page/portal Q&A —— every "is this a fit / what do I write / what does this field want" call.
  • 27.2.2. Auditor (SA3, LLM): the semantic CL review you correctly say code can't do —— false claims, stance/emphasis, overall quality, decision precision.
  • 27.2.3. Code (linter v2): only the deterministic slice —— dashes/+, section numbers, P.S. tail, employer-name match, figure-vs-profile facts, salary/notice answers.
  • 27.3. So it's code orchestrates → LLMs judge → code verifies-what's-verifiable. The PD being code doesn't remove intelligence; it removes the intelligence from the one place (the loop) where drift was fatal.
  • 4.4 (fork SA1 once-primed, then per-card forks with full context, no re-reading): you are RIGHT, and it converges with what I proposed.
  • 28.1. Your insight —— SA1 needs no session continuity; card 2 need not know card 1 —— is exactly the property that makes fresh-per-card safe. Confirmed.
  • 28.2. Two implementations of the SAME principle:
  • 28.2.1. Your fork model: prime a session on the context once, fork per card. The SDK supports session resume/fork; prompt-caching makes the shared prefix ~free on each fork.
  • 28.2.2. My scoped-prompt model: the orchestrator hands each worker only its slice (CL rules + profile + rubric verdict + THIS job's text), never the 111KB.
  • 28.3. Difference: mine gives the worker LESS (only what one card needs) so it's even leaner; yours gives the worker the FULL primed context cheaply. Both avoid re-reading; both give fresh context per card. We'll use whichever measures cheaper at P6.1 —— likely a hybrid (fork a small primed base that holds the stable CL/profile rules, inject the per-card job text).
  • 28.4. Correction to my earlier framing (r2 pt 21): "fresh worker doesn't re-read" is right, but your "read once then fork" is the cleaner mental model —— adopted.
  • 4.6 (let a struggling SA1 keep going whilst PD moves on): yes, and this is the design's strength.
  • 29.1. Because each worker owns ONE card, a worker stuck on a hard portal is isolated —— it cannot stall the system. The PD watches its token use and either lets it finish or kills it on a ceiling, meanwhile advancing the queue.
  • 29.2. Serial mode (default, 1 worker): trivially fine —— PD just times out and re-queues.
  • 29.3. Your worry (multiple struggling SA1s under parallel scaling): handled by the worker-POOL abstraction (scaffolded, not active). Each worker is independent; a struggler is one occupied slot; the PD applies the same retire triggers per worker. No SA2/SA3 fan-out problem because SA2/SA3 are code, scaling to N workers for free.

  • 30.2. TWO real bugs found: (a) the ⏳_-retained-under-❌_ hygiene bug on all 4 _moved_pending files (❌_⏳_...); (b) one genuine mismatch —— ❌_UBER_... is voided but its Outcome still says "Applying" (not a recorded void).
  • 30.3. Rebuild rules (added to DevPlan P2.6.9): every void writes a machine-readable reason to the ledger AND an AR trailing note; prefix transitions are code-owned so ❌_ ALWAYS strips ⏳_; no _moved_* suffix lingers in applied/. Void reasons become queryable, not archaeological.

  • 31.1. The new AJAP runs as a standalone process. It exposes a COCKPIT via files:

- 4.3. Autonomy breaches → browser-failure fallbacks are code paths (struggle → Pending → continue), never "ask the user".
- 4.4. Worker liveness → the orchestrator `await`s each worker call under asyncio timeouts; dual-SA races and invisible overruns cannot occur.
- 4.5. Scoring misroutes + CL fabrication → rubric/routing as pure functions w/ unit tests; linter v2 adds factual checks (re 15.3).
